title: An IDF delegation set up a field clinic in the city of Minamisanriku in Japan after the tsunami and handed it over to the city

trailer.text: On March 11, 2011, a massive earthquake struck Japan, followed by a tsunami.
In the city of Minamisanriku, according to Mayor Sato, 70 percent of the buildings were razed to the ground.
On March 28, a delegation of the IDF Home Front Command and Medical Corps arrived in the city, and the following day it opened an advanced clinic.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the team treated more than 200 patients in two weeks.
On April 10, the delegation left Japan, having handed over a functioning field hospital to the local authorities.

paragraphs.text: At roughly 3 pm, a massive earthquake was detected east of Japan, and a severe tsunami warning was issued for the residents of the coast.
The official warning spoke of a six-meter wave, but the tsunami was almost three times higher.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the Great East Japan Earthquake claimed more than 18,000 lives.
According to JNS, on March 11, 2011, 12,000 people lived in the fishing village of Minamisanriku.
According to Mayor Sato, the community lost 831 people, and 70 percent of the buildings were razed to the ground.
The mayor himself said that the wave swept him to a staircase and that he broke two ribs.
Roads were blocked or destroyed, the power grid and the cellular network were down, and the water supply was disrupted.
According to the local doctor Nishizawa, the medical facilities had been destroyed, and more medical teams arrived only after a week.
Zuckerman, deputy head of the Israeli delegation, said that only the structure was left of the local hospital, and everything else had been washed away and burned.
According to him, almost no doctors were left in the town, certainly not specialists, and only residents remained.

stations.title: The offer, the invitation and the permit

paragraphs.text: Prime Minister Netanyahu quickly offered aid to the victims of the earthquake.
According to Algemeiner, Israel was one of the first countries to offer Japan help immediately after the disaster.
The government of Japan made foreign assistance contingent on the teams bringing their own equipment, and Israel was the only country that met this requirement on short notice.
According to the Jerusalem Post, Israel's ambassador to Japan asked Monden to find out whether a municipal government would agree to accept an IDF medical team.
According to the Jerusalem Post, in the 1960s a 23-year-old young Japanese man named Isamu Sato very much wanted to be accepted into a kibbutz in Israel.

Also according to the Jerusalem Post, the mayor of Kurihara, Sato, remembered the promise he had made in Israel decades earlier to promote friendship between Israel and Japan, and decided to receive the delegation.
The mayor was told that the team would arrive as a self-contained unit, so that the community would not have to provide it with food or other necessities.
According to Zuckerman, a law in Japan prohibits receiving medical treatment from foreign caregivers.
The Japanese parliament held a special session to give the members of the delegation a special permit to treat the residents.
According to the Jerusalem Post, of all the foreign teams, only the doctors of the Israeli delegation were allowed to treat patients without a Japanese medical license.
On March 21, a preliminary Home Front Command delegation, two doctors and an officer, arrived in Miyagi Prefecture to assess the needs.
Israel also sent aid, from blankets and coats to chemical toilets, to roughly 500,000 people left homeless after the disaster.
The first equipment shipment included 10,000 coats, 6,000 blankets, 8,000 pairs of gloves and 150 portable toilets.
On March 28, the IDF Home Front Command and Medical Corps delegation arrived in Minamisanriku.
The city lies 310 miles north of Tokyo.
According to JNS, the IDF delegation was the first foreign relief delegation to arrive at the site.
The delegation brought all the equipment from Israel, even fuel, because people could not get to a doctor after they had run out of fuel.
It included doctors, nurses and X-ray specialists, and upon arrival it immediately began setting up a field hospital.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the team numbered nearly 50 people, among them also pharmacists and Japanese-speaking interpreters.
The deputy head of the delegation said that the medical center was set up within four hours of arrival.
The emergency clinic was built from six prefab buildings.
The day after arrival, an advanced clinic opened with pediatrics, surgery, maternity and gynecology, otolaryngology, optometry, a laboratory, a pharmacy and an intensive care unit.

According to a JDC press release of March 24, 2011, the organization cooperated with the IDF field hospital that was to operate in Minamisanriku, and intended to provide equipment such as an infant ventilator, a portable ultrasound, antibiotics and other medications.
The clinic's first patient was the mayor, and he was examined by the commander of the medical delegation, Col. Dr. Ofir Cohen-Marom.
According to a Walla report, the mayor asked for an X-ray of his ribs, and the X-ray showed that he had no fractures.
When he learned of the plight of the pregnant women in the area, a doctor from the delegation who was trained in delivering babies began making house calls, accompanied by a local nurse.
Nishizawa said that the Israelis' expertise was amazing and that everything was up and running at record speed.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the team treated more than 200 patients in two weeks.
According to a Walla report, the delegation was prohibited from giving patients Israeli medications that are not recognized in Japan.
Also according to Walla, on Wednesday, March 30, 2011, few patients came to the clinic, and from midday on almost no patients came at all.
According to the Jerusalem Post, on April 7 an aftershock hit the area.
The members of the delegation decided that if the accumulated radiation exceeded 30 millirem, they would evacuate the area.
According to Japan's Headquarters for Earthquake Research Promotion, on April 7, 2011 at 23:32 (Japan time), a magnitude 7.1 earthquake occurred.
Members of the delegation played soccer with children from the city.
According to a report by the Japanese Foreign Ministry, the delegation's smooth operation would not have been possible without the assistance of Kurihara City.
According to a Walla report, the mayor of Kurihara studied at the University of Haifa 38 years ago, and has respected Israelis ever since.
According to Walla, all the Japanese media networks covered the delegation's activity extensively.
The team offered to donate all the equipment it had brought, including an X-ray machine and a portable ultrasound unit.
According to a Walla report, the delegation left the city's residents a large amount of equipment donated by the Foreign Ministry.
According to the article in Israel Hayom, on April 10, a month after the disaster, the delegation left Japan, after handing over a functioning field hospital to the local authorities.

According to the Jerusalem Post, at the farewell party Mayor Sato, who is not the mayor of Minamisanriku (who was the first patient at the clinic), said that the clinic they had left behind would be a cornerstone in the restoration of the city.
According to a Walla report, the mayor promised that the clinic compound would serve as the basis for the new local hospital that would replace the one that was destroyed.
In an interview conducted about a decade after the disaster, Mayor Sato said that the biggest challenge is to get back up and restore the sense of community.
Two years after the tsunami, the residents of Minamisanriku inaugurated a statue honoring the assistance Israel provided the city.
The statue was created by the Israeli artist David Susanna, and was installed in front of the municipal offices and the temporary Israeli hospitals in the city.
Today, a memorial donated by Israel stands where the hospital was.
The mayor said that the city's residents sent the Israeli embassy a letter of thanks to all Israelis.
Nishizawa said that Israel will always be remembered as the first country that came to their rescue, and that it gave them a feeling of connection to the rest of the world.
Israel's ambassador to Japan said that they had the honor of assisting the residents and of being the first to provide medical aid.

claims.quote: They even played a soccer game with local children.

claims.quote: A report compiled by the Japanese Foreign Ministry a few months later stated that the IDF medical team's smooth operation in Minamisanriku could not have been possible without the assistance from Kurihara City.

claims.text: לפי כתבת וואלה, ראש עיריית קוריארה למד באוניברסיטת חיפה לפני 38 שנים ומאז מכבד את הישראלים.
claims.quote: ראש עיריית קוריארה, שלפני 38 שנים למד באוניברסיטת חיפה ומאז מכבד את הישראלים

claims.text: לפי כתבת וואלה, כל רשתות התקשורת היפניות סיקרו את פעילות המשלחת בהרחבה.
claims.quote: כל רשתות התקשורת היפניות סיקרו את פועלנו בהרחבה.

claims.text: הצוות הציע לתרום את כל הציוד שהביא, כמו מכשיר רנטגן ומכשיר אולטרסאונד נייד.
claims.quote: They offered to donate all the equipment they had brought in, such as X-ray machine and portable ultrasound unit.

claims.text: לפי כתבת וואלה, המשלחת השאירה ציוד רב שנתרם על ידי משרד החוץ לתושבי העיר.
claims.quote: והשארנו ציוד רב, שנתרם על ידי משרד החוץ לתושבי העיר

claims.text: במסיבת הפרידה אמר ראש העיר סאטו שהמרפאה שהשאירו תהיה אבן יסוד בשיקום העיר.
claims.quote: The clinic you left behind will be a cornerstone in the restoration of our city, which suffered a major disaster.

claims.text: לפי כתבת וואלה, ראש העיר הבטיח שמתחם המרפאה ישמש בסיס לבית החולים המקומי החדש במקום זה שנהרס.
claims.quote: אשר מבטיח לנו כי מתחם המרפאה יהווה, החל ביום חמישי, את הבסיס לבית החולים המקומי החדש

claims.text: ראש העיר סאטו אמר שהאתגר הגדול הוא לשקם את תחושת הקהילה.
claims.quote: Our biggest challenge is getting back up and recreating the sense of community

claims.text: היום ניצבת באתר בית החולים לשעבר אנדרטה שתרמה ישראל.
claims.quote: Today, a memorial stands on the grounds of the former facility, donated by Israel.

claims.text: ראש העיר סיפר שבשנה שעברה שלחו תושבי העיר לשגרירות ישראל מכתב תודה לכל הישראלים.
claims.quote: Last year, we wrote a letter of thanks to all Israelis and had it sent to the Israeli embassy.

claims.text: נישיזאווה אמר שישראל תיזכר תמיד כמדינה הראשונה שבאה לעזרתם ונתנה להם תחושה של קשר לשאר העולם.
claims.quote: will always be remembered as the first country that came to our rescue and gave us the feeling that we are connected to the rest of the world.

claims.text: שגרירת ישראל ביפן אמרה שהיה להם הכבוד לסייע לתושבים ולהיות הראשונים שסיפקו סיוע רפואי.
claims.quote: היה לנו הכבוד לסייע לתושבים המקומיים לפני 10 שנים ולהיות הראשונים שמספקים סיוע רפואי.

claims.text: לפי eJewishPhilanthropy, ישראל הקימה את בית החולים השדה הראשון שהוקם ביפן על ידי מדינה זרה בעקבות רעידת האדמה והצונאמי.
claims.quote: Israel is stepping up its assistance to Japan by establishing the first field hospital set up by an outside country in order to provide assistance following the recent earthquake and tsunami.

claims.text: לפי מאמר ב-American Journal of Disaster Medicine, המשלחת הרפואית הייתה הצוות הזר הראשון שנפרס ביפן.
claims.quote: After well-coordinated diplomatic efforts, our medical delegation was the first foreign team to deploy in Japan.

claims.text: לפי כתבת וואלה, המשלחת הישראלית הייתה המשלחת הזרה היחידה באזור.
claims.quote: למעשה, אנו המשלחת הזרה היחידה פה וזה בהחלט כבוד רב למדינת ישראל.

claims.text: לפי צוקרמן, לפני האסון מנתה מינאמיסנריקו כ-17,000 איש וכעת נותרו בה כ-2,000.
claims.quote: לפני האסון, מנימי סן ריקו מנתה כ- 17,000 איש, אך כעת נותרו בה רק כ-2,000 איש.

claims.text: לפי כתבת וואלה, ראש העיר סיפר שמחצית מ-17 אלף התושבים נהרגו או נעלמו ומחצית מהניצולים חסרי בית.
claims.quote: הוא מספר לנו שמחצית מ?17 אלף תושבי המקום נהרגו או נעלמו ושמחצית מהניצולים הם חסרי בית.

claims.text: לפי כתבת וואלה, היפנים הנפיקו אישור מיוחד שמאפשר לרופאים זרים לטפל ביפנים.
claims.quote: הם הנפיקו אישור מיוחד המאפשר לרופאים זרים לטפל ביפנים!

claims.text: לפי הוועדה היפנית לקידום מחקר רעידות אדמה, ב-7 באפריל 2011 בשעה 23:32 (שעון יפן) אירעה רעידת אדמה בעוצמה 7.1.
claims.quote: On April 7, 2011 at 23:32 (JST), there was a M7.1 earthquake

quote_translations.c34: We even brought fuel from Israel, because there are people here who cannot see a doctor, simply because they ran out of fuel
quote_translations.c26: We set up the medical center in the town of Minami Sanriku within four hours of arriving at the site.
quote_translations.c32: He injured his ribs when the tsunami wave swept the coast, and he asks for an X-ray to check whether he has fractures. He was examined and it was found that he has no fractures.

quote_translations.c38: All in all, few patients came, and from the afternoon there is an almost complete halt in the flow of patients.

quote_translations.c44: Who promises us that the clinic compound will form, starting on Thursday, the basis for the new local hospital
quote_translations.c58: We had the honor of assisting the local residents 10 years ago and of being the first to provide medical aid.
